lead: Black-box testing designs test cases from the written specification only, without looking at the code. You treat the program as a closed box: feed it inputs, read the outputs, compare with what the specification promised. It exists because most defects a user suffers are visible behaviour — a wrong total, a missing check, a wrong message — and because these tests survive a rewrite. Two techniques choose the inputs. Equivalence partitioning groups inputs that should behave alike, and boundary value analysis tests the edges of those groups. Functional testers use both on booking forms, UPI screens and login pages.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.1 for test cases and expected results, and Unit 2 (the SRS) for the input rules this chapter turns into tests.

blocks.text: The specification is the only source. A black-box test case is an input plus the output the specification promises for it. You never read the code, so the same tests still work after the code is rewritten.

Black-box testing is also called functional, specification-based or behavioural testing. White-box testing (Chapter 4.3) measures how much code a test suite executes. Black-box testing measures how much of the specification the suite checks.

The input domain is the set of all values one input item can receive. The output domain is the set of all results the program can produce. A specification states both as rules: age is an integer from 1 to 120; a PIN is exactly four digits.
Strength: it catches wrong visible behaviour — a wrong fare, a missing validation, a wrong message. Weakness: it cannot say which lines of code no test reached. Use both kinds.

Inputs in the same class should be handled the same way: same validation, same route through the rules, same kind of output. If one value in the class finds a defect, the others probably would too. So one representative value per class is enough.

items: List every input item and its rule from the specification.
Split each input domain into valid classes (accepted) and invalid classes (rejected).
Give each class an ID, C1, C2 and so on, and pick one representative value from each.

For a single input item, write one test case per class with its expected output, so the count equals the number of classes. With several input items, cover all valid classes of one input in the same case where possible, and use one case per invalid class; the count is the largest number of valid classes for any one input plus the total number of invalid classes.
For invalid classes use one invalid value per test case.
Range a to b: one valid class (a to b), two invalid classes (below a, above b).
A list that accepts up to n items gives three classes: 0 items, 1 to n items, and more than n items.

A yes/no input where both answers are allowed gives two valid classes, true and false. False is an invalid class only when the rule requires yes, for example a terms-and-conditions box that must be ticked.
A set of allowed codes: one valid class per code, plus one invalid class for any other code.

blocks.text: Defects cluster at the edges of a class. A programmer writes age ≥ 1 and age ≤ 120, or slips and writes > 1. The middle of the range almost never fails; the values at and just outside the limit do.

blocks.where: a is the lowest accepted value and b the highest; a−1 and b+1 are the values just outside the valid range.

blocks.text: With a = 1 and b = 120 the values are 0, 1, 2, 119, 120, 121. Some syllabi call the extra outer values a−1 and b+1 robustness testing.

Boundaries also sit inside a range wherever behaviour changes. The age rule changes at 60, so 59, 60 and 61 are boundary values too. Testing 60 alone does not show whether 59 wrongly gets the discount.
Partition first, then take the boundaries of each class. Do not drop the invalid classes: test 0 and 121, not only 1, 2, 119 and 120.
When two or more rules interact, a decision table lists the conditions and the action for every combination. Two yes/no conditions give 2² = 4 rules, so at least four test cases.
Each column becomes one test case; strike out columns that cannot occur. Combinatorial and pairwise testing, which pick combinations of many inputs automatically, are left to tools.

spec.aria: A band split into four classes: below 1 rejected, 1 to 59 accepted, 60 to 120 accepted with discount, above 120 rejected. Under it a line with dots at 0, 1, 2, 59, 60, 61, 119, 120 and 121.

examples.question: A railway booking form accepts a passenger's age as an integer from 1 to 120. A passenger aged 60 or more gets the senior discount. (a) List the equivalence classes. (b) List the boundary values for the range 1 to 120. (c) Give test cases for the ages 0, 1, 2, 59, 60, 61, 119, 120 and 121, with the expected result for each.
steps: Read the rules: valid age is an integer from 1 to 120, and the discount starts at 60. Behaviour changes at three places: 1 (start of the valid range), 60 (discount start) and 120 (end of the range).

(a) Classes: C1 = age below 1, invalid, rejected. C2 = 1 to 59, valid, accepted without discount. C3 = 60 to 120, valid, accepted with discount. C4 = age above 120, invalid, rejected. That is 4 classes.
(c) The nine values 0, 1, 2, 59, 60, 61, 119, 120, 121 are all different, so they give 9 test cases.
Expected results: 0 rejected; 1, 2 and 59 accepted without discount; 60, 61, 119 and 120 accepted with discount; 121 rejected.
Each of the nine cases checks what the specification fixes: the form accepts or rejects the age, and for 60 to 120 it shows the senior discount message.
examples.answer: Four equivalence classes and nine boundary test cases: 0 and 121 rejected, 1, 2 and 59 accepted without discount, 60, 61, 119 and 120 accepted with the senior discount.
examples.check:
lo, hi, senior = 1, 120, 60
classes = [
    ("C1 below 1", "reject"),
    ("C2 1 to 59", "accept, no discount"),
    ("C3 60 to 120", "accept, discount"),
    ("C4 above 120", "reject"),
]
print(len(classes))
tests = sorted(set([lo - 1, lo, lo + 1, hi - 1, hi, hi + 1,
                    senior - 1, senior, senior + 1]))
print(len(tests))
for t in tests:
    print(t)

traps: Testing only a middle value of a valid range and never testing the invalid classes, so nothing is learnt about rejection.
Missing an internal boundary such as 60 when the requirement has two rules; 60 is a boundary, not just the ends 1 and 120.
Writing the boundary list off by one: for 1 to 120 it is 0, 1, 2, 119, 120, 121, not 1, 2, 119, 120 and not 0, 1, 120, 121.
Putting two invalid values in one test case; the first rejection can stop the check, so the second is never exercised.
Mixing up the two techniques: equivalence partitioning takes any representative of a class, boundary value analysis deliberately takes the edges.

quiz.q: Define black-box testing and give two other names for it.
quiz.a: Testing that designs cases only from the specification, without reading the code. Also called functional, specification-based or behavioural testing.

quiz.q: An input range is 10 to 50. List its boundary values.
Why is one test per equivalence class usually enough?
quiz.a: All values in a class follow the same rule and produce the same kind of result, so a second value from the same class tests the same rule again.

quiz.q: Why can black-box testing not tell you which lines of code no test executed?
quiz.a: The tester never sees the code, so statement and path coverage are unknown; only white-box testing measures them.

quiz.q: A form accepts a quantity as an integer from 1 to 10. Give the equivalence classes and the boundary values.
quiz.a: Classes: below 1 invalid, 1 to 10 valid, above 10 invalid, so 3 classes. Boundaries: 0, 1, 2, 9, 10, 11, so 6 values.

quiz.q: A salary field accepts 10000 to 50000 rupees and a bonus applies from 30000. List the boundary test values.
quiz.a: Range: 9999, 10000, 10001, 49999, 50000, 50001. Internal bonus edge: 29999, 30000, 30001. All nine values are distinct, so nine test cases.

quiz.q: A tester submits age 0 and age 121 in the same form. Why is this a poor test?
quiz.a: The form may stop at the first invalid field, so the second invalid class is never checked. One invalid class per test case keeps each rejection visible.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real forms have several inputs, and testing every combination explodes: five fields with five values each give 3125 cases. Pairwise and combinatorial testing pick a small set of combinations that covers every pair of values at least once, and tools generate the cases. Model-based testing builds cases from a state machine of the specification, and property-based testing generates random inputs and checks that stated properties hold. Search next: pairwise testing, classification tree method, model-based testing, property-based testing.
